messages.subject: New analysis tool for seabird at-sea data
messages.subject_clean: New analysis tool for seabird at-sea data
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

A quick note to mention our R package GeoAviR and web app GeoAviRWeb for the computation of seabird at-sea densities. This initiative is from the Canadian Wildlife Service and Université du Québec à Rimouski. This tool originally has been built for our continuously growing seabird at-sea database in eastern Canada and compute densities by species in one run. Since there is no restriction on access, any user can import his own data and do line-transect or strip-transect analyses for data collected using binned distances. You can access our web app and R package at GeoAviRWeb.ddns.net <http://GeoAviRWeb.ddns.net>. We also have a google group: https://groups.google.com/d/forum/geoavir

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
messages.body_plain:
Variability in cluster size does not invalidate the arithmetic mean, nor justify use of the geometric mean.  However, size bias means that the arithmetic mean tends to be biased high.  (Larger groups are more likely to be detected, so the mean size of detected groups is larger than the mean size of all groups.)  The default method in Distance corrects for size bias.  Instead of the arithmetic mean, it uses regression of log cluster size on estimated probability of detection to predict mean cluster size when detection is certain (as there can be no size bias when all clusters are detected).  I can see no reason to prefer the geometric mean over this option.  If you really want to use the geometric mean, you can calculate it outside Distance, and include it as a multiplier in the analysis.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
messages.body_plain:
There is another aspect to group (cluster) size which we meet with in (low level, oblique) aerial census, namely counting bias. While a larger group is easier to detect than a smaller group (detection bias) a larger group is more difficult to count (counting bias). More animals are missed when counting larger groups than smaller groups, i.e. counting bias is positively associated with group size. We address this problem in aerial census in three ways: first, by using a fixed width of counting strip to minimise and hold constant detection bias, second by photographing groups >~10 to count later in the laboratory, and third by applying species/habitat group size correction factors. The fixed strip holds detection bias constant so we can concentrate on the big problem which is counting bias. Even so, we are still underestimating, especially with densely grouped species such as buffalo and livestock.

These subtle and difficult interactions between detection and counting bias may have an important effect on distance methods. For example, a group quite near to an observer and counted carefully many times to be 30 animals may well be "only" 32, while a group quite some way from the same observer and also counted equally carefully to be 30 animals may well be 36. Simply accounting for detection bias leaves counting bias unresolved.

We have recently been involved in an aerial census of Khulan and gazelle in 150,000 km2 of the Gobi desert, Mongolia,  (http://southgobi2013.countingstuff.org) using high resolution (2.5cm GSD) sample aerial photography (APS sampling). At exactly the same time a ground census using distance sampling overlapped in a 90,000km2 area. We have significant problems reconciling the two sets of census data. The output of the ground census seems worryingly sensitive to model parameterisation. In contrast, the aerial census database is built like a brick ----house and can take anything you can throw at it -- which is not the same as saying it is not "wrong"!

Best regards, Mike

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
messages.body_plain:
Mike, yes, counting bias is a major problem.  With terrestrial or ship surveys, counting bias tends to be a function of distance from the line or point.  If you can assume no bias at zero distance, then the default regression method in the software Distance corrects for this bias as well as for detection bias.  However, in aerial surveys, that is unlikely to be the case, and the same is true of terrestrial surveys when groups flee from the observer before a good count can be made.

For aerial surveys, as technology improves, I expect observers to be replaced by high-resolution imagery surveys.  The aircraft can then fly higher, avoiding responsive movement.  Detectability tends not to fall off with distance, as the distance to the outer edge of the strip is much the same as directly below the aircraft (combination of high altitude and relatively narrow strip).  Data are available for validation, and correcting for mis-identifications and under-counting.  Availability remains an issue (e.g. diving animals for marine surveys, or animals hidden by canopy), but can be addressed.

If you have known-size groups, you can compare observer estimates with the known sizes, to estimate a correction.  E.g. for shipboard surveys, a helicopter taking photos of some of the groups might provide the known-sizes.  For terrestrial surveys, some groups might be watched from vantage points, while an observer is sent past.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Resample sample or observations within samples for model averaging
messages.subject_clean: Resample sample or observations within samples for model averaging
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am running in CDS engine a model averaging but I am not quite sure if for my data is better to select resampling samples or observations within samples. I got three plausible models for male birds distance data (25 transect lines of different lenghts) with strong spatial aggregation, so I applied post-stratification with overlapping strata to calculate a less biased encounter rate variance. However, when using model average my confidence interval and CV are very large in comparison to using samples as the resampling replicates.Most of my transect lines have no bird detections, so resampling samples seems very prone to generate large variation.

This is the first time I am doing model averaging in Distance, so I am not sure on how to select between these two options based on my type of data.

Thanks in advance for any help.

Sergio

Well, after no answer I decided not to use bootstrap and calculate with Jeff's functions in RMark model averaged estimates along with variance using Burnham & Anderson (2002) book's equations and tail area CIs as described by Turek & Fletcher (2012). It could be great if these calculations and AIC weights can be implemented in next versions of Distance program as well as bootstrap approximation with variable probabilities depending on the size of transect lines; all my samples were of variable distances (km) and the program was considering equal probabilities for each of those...

Please if anyone have any suggestion I would appreciate that.

Sergio

messages.subject: Mulitple helicopters cause detection function woes
messages.subject_clean: Mulitple helicopters cause detection function woes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am looking for some guidance on what (if anything) Distance folks think could be done with some messy data I have.

We flew an aerial moose survey. Due to a variety of reasons beyond our control, we had to use 3 different helicopters over the course of the survey. This resulted in detection functions that look very different depending on the model of the helicopter (see attached). In particular one has very bad behavior near 0. Another issue is that each helicopter model was only used for a day or two, and so only sampled part of the survey area (see attached map). We do have some data from an adjoining study area that was also surveyed around the same time. Could this possibly be used to help fit the detection function? What other analysis options do I have?

Any advice would be appreciated. Even if it is a stern: "Do not analyze this mess!".

Of note, the first three days were done using EC-120/EC-130 helicopters and the last day was done using a Jet Ranger. The Jet Ranger is what we have used with success in the past. The results of this survey suggest that it is also what we stick with going forward!

Thanks,
Hannah

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Abridged summary of distance-sampling@googlegroups.com - 1 update in 1 topic
messages.body_plain:
Hannah-

They don't look terrible to me. That amount of variability with n=25 and 43 is to be expected. You should try generating a n of 25 or 43 from the absolute value of a normal and then look at it with the intervals you used.

Here is one such picture. In R I used abs(rnorm(25,0,200)). You may be surprised by the variability. It does look like you may have some rounding to values 100, 200 etc but since you didn't say how distance was measured I'm not sure if that is reasonable.

--jeff

messages.subject: User survey 2015 results
messages.body_plain:
Hi distance samplers,

Thanks to everyone who contributed their thoughts to the 2015 user
survey. The quantitative answers have been plotted and you can look at
them here:

http://distancesampling.org/user-survey/results-2015.html

The development team met yesterday to look over the results and we are
making plans to address the issues you raised, as well as start to
analyse the long-form answers you provided. We'll post more updates on
this list and on distancesampling.org <http://distancesampling.org> and contact those who wished to be
contacted about helping out directly.

Thanks again to all those who took part!

cheers,
--dave (on behalf of the Distance Development Team)
